people.name: Sun Yung Shin
body: In 2016 a Minneapolis poet edited a book that asked Minnesotans to talk honestly about race in their own state. A Good Time for the Truth: Race in Minnesota, edited by Sun Yung Shin, collected essays by writers of color living in a place that likes to call itself progressive.

Shin was born in Seoul, adopted by American parents and raised in the Chicago area. Her story is part of a larger one. Korean children began arriving in Minnesota for adoption in 1955, and the Minnesota Historical Society reports that the state now has the highest concentration of Korean adoptees of any state.

Shin made Minnesota her home. In 2005 she finished a master's degree in secondary education at the University of St. Thomas in St. Paul. She lives in Minneapolis, where she co-directs the organization Poetry Asylum with the poet Su Hwang. Her first poetry collection, Skirt Full of Black (Coffee House Press, 2007), won the Asian American Literary Award for poetry. Rough, and Savage followed in 2012. Unbearable Splendor (2016) won the Minnesota Book Award for poetry, and Coffee House Press published The Wet Hex in 2022.

Shin has also edited books about adoption itself. She co-edited Outsiders Within: Writing on Transracial Adoption (South End Press, 2006), an anthology written by adoptees rather than about them. She has written for children too, starting with the bilingual Korean and English Cooper's Lesson (Children's Book Press, 2004). She has received support from the Bush Foundation, the McKnight Foundation, the Jerome Foundation and the Minnesota State Arts Board.
keyFacts: Born in Seoul; adopted by American parents and raised in the Chicago area.

2006: Co-edited Outsiders Within: Writing on Transracial Adoption.
2007: Skirt Full of Black, which won the Asian American Literary Award for poetry.
2016: Edited A Good Time for the Truth: Race in Minnesota; published Unbearable Splendor, which won the Minnesota Book Award for poetry.
2022: The Wet Hex.

people.name: Jane Jeong Trenka
body: In September 1972 a Korean baby was sent for adoption to Minnesota. She grew up with an American family in small-town Minnesota, earned perfect grades and trained as a concert pianist. By the Minnesota Historical Society Press's account of her memoir, she also learned not to ask about the mother who had given her away. That child was Jane Jeong Trenka.

Trenka graduated magna cum laude from Augsburg College in Minneapolis, with degrees in music performance and English literature. While she was at university on a music scholarship, a fellow student began to stalk her, and his obsession escalated into a plot to kill her. The ordeal stirred up years of questions she had pushed down. She searched for her own identity, confronted her American family, fought the adoption agency's bureaucracy and got to know her mother and sisters in Seoul again.

She told this story in The Language of Blood (Minnesota Historical Society Press, 2003). It won the Minnesota Book Award for Autobiography/Memoir and was a Barnes & Noble Discover Great New Writers selection. Before it came out she had won the Brenda Ueland Prize, a Loft Creative Non-Fiction Award, a SASE/Jerome Award and a Minnesota State Arts Board fellowship.

Trenka returned to Korea in 2004. With Julia Sudbury and Sun Yung Shin she co-edited Outsiders Within: Writing on Transracial Adoption (2006), and Graywolf Press published her second memoir, Fugitive Visions: An Adoptee's Return to Korea, in 2009. In Seoul she served as a volunteer president of TRACK (Truth and Reconciliation for the Adoption Community of Korea), which pushed for full disclosure of past and present Korean adoption practices. PBS's POV describes a 2008 complaint TRACK brought to South Korea's Anti-Corruption and Civil Rights Commission and a 2009 coalition effort to revise the adoption law. In 2012 The Korea Times reported on her work supporting single mothers, who she said faced pressure to give up their children.
keyFacts: September 1972: Sent for adoption from Korea to Minnesota.
Graduated magna cum laude from Augsburg College.
2003: The Language of Blood; Minnesota Book Award for Autobiography/Memoir.
2004: Returned to Korea.
2006: Co-edited Outsiders Within with Julia Sudbury and Sun Yung Shin.
2009: Fugitive Visions (Graywolf Press).
Served as president of TRACK in Seoul.

people.name: Ed Bok Lee
body: In 2012 a book of poems from a Minneapolis press won both the American Book Award and the Minnesota Book Award. The book was Whorled, by Ed Bok Lee.
Lee grew up in South Korea, North Dakota and Minnesota. He earned an MFA from Brown University and teaches at Metropolitan State University in St. Paul.

His first collection, Real Karaoke People (New Rivers Press, 2005), won a PEN/Open Book Award and the Members' Choice Asian American Literary Award. Coffee House Press published Whorled in 2011 and Mitochondrial Night in 2019. He also translates Korean poetry. With Eun-Mi Yang he co-translated Hail, Che!, by the Korean poet Pak Jeong-de, published by Black Ocean in 2025.

2011: Whorled (Coffee House Press).

people.name: Kim Park Nelson
body: Between 2003 and 2006 Kim Park Nelson collected 73 oral histories from Korean adoptees in the United States and around the world. She also developed and taught what the U.S.-Korea Institute's biography of her calls the first college course on Korean adoption in the United States.

POV reports that Park Nelson was adopted from South Korea in 1971. She earned a Ph.D. in American Studies from the University of Minnesota, and went on to teach American Multicultural Studies at Minnesota State University Moorhead. As of 2023, Korean Quarterly reported that she had been a professor of American Studies at Winona State University for about two years, after 13 years at Moorhead, and that a Bush Fellowship starting August 1, 2023, would let her study how disabled members, members of color and queer members can gain more influence in their unions. A University of Minnesota biography from around 2021 says she has also served as Equity Inclusion Coordinator for the InterFaculty Organization, the faculty union of the Minnesota State university system.

Her book Invisible Asians: Korean American Adoptees, Asian American Experiences, and Racial Exceptionalism came out from Rutgers University Press in 2016. It draws on interviews with more than sixty adult Korean adoptees in Minnesota, the Pacific Northwest and Seoul. She points out that earlier research mostly asked adoptive parents about adoption, and argues that adoptees should be asked themselves. The book looks at how adoptees can be racially "invisible," often treated as white or as an exception in their families and communities.

Park Nelson was a lead organizer of the International Symposia on Korean Adoption Studies in Seoul. She has taken her research to Minnesota audiences outside universities too, including public programs at regional libraries in northwestern Minnesota in 2017, funded by the state's Legacy Amendment.
keyFacts: 1971: Adopted from South Korea.
2003–2006: Collected 73 oral histories from Korean adoptees.
Ph.D. in American Studies, University of Minnesota.
2016: Invisible Asians (Rutgers University Press).
2017: Legacy-funded library programs in northwestern Minnesota.
As of 2023: Professor of American Studies at Winona State University, after 13 years at Moorhead.
2023: Named a Bush Fellow, with the fellowship starting August 1.

people.name: Philip Jaisohn
body: In April 1896 a newspaper appeared in Seoul using the Korean alphabet, Hangul, rather than Chinese characters. It was called Tongnip Sinmun, or The Independent, and its founder was a doctor who had just come back from America.

Seo Jae-pil was born in Boseong County, Korea, in January 1864. As a young reformer he took part in the Gapsin Coup, an attempt to modernize the Joseon government, which failed. The Korea Times and EBSCO date the coup to 1884; the Philip Jaisohn Memorial Foundation says 1885. He fled the country and reached San Francisco in 1885. In the United States he took the name Philip Jaisohn. In 1890 he became a naturalized U.S. citizen, the first Korean to do so, according to EBSCO. In 1892 he earned a medical degree from Columbian Medical College, now George Washington University.

Jaisohn went back to Korea and launched The Independent on April 7, 1896. He also helped found the Independence Club that year, which pushed for reform and Korean sovereignty. He later returned to the United States and settled in the Philadelphia area. After the March First Movement of 1919, a nationwide protest against Japanese colonial rule in Korea, he helped convene the First Korean Congress in Philadelphia that April to rally support for Korean independence.
He died on January 5, 1951, in Norristown, Pennsylvania. The Philip Jaisohn Memorial Foundation, founded in Philadelphia in 1975, carries on health and community service in his name.
keyFacts: 1864: Born in January in Boseong County, Korea.
1885: Reached San Francisco after a failed coup.
1890: Became a naturalized U.S. citizen.
1892: M.D., Columbian Medical College (now George Washington University).
1896: Founded The Independent; first issue April 7.
1919: First Korean Congress, Philadelphia, in April.
1951: Died January 5 in Norristown, Pennsylvania.

people.name: Sammy Lee
body: As a boy in Highland Park, Los Angeles, Sammy Lee could swim at the nearby Pasadena public pool only one day a week. That was Wednesday, called "International Day," when children of color were allowed in. To keep training, his coach dug a sand pit in his backyard for him to practice his jumps.

Lee was born on August 1, 1920, in Fresno, California, to Korean immigrant parents. He studied at Occidental College while competing as a diver, and he earned his M.D. from the University of Southern California in 1947. At the 1948 London Olympics he won gold in 10-meter platform diving and bronze on the 3-meter springboard, which made him the first Asian American man to win Olympic gold for the United States. At the 1952 Helsinki Games he won the platform gold again, the first man to win back-to-back Olympic platform titles. In 1953 he received the Sullivan Award as the nation's top amateur athlete. From 1953 to 1955 he served in the U.S. Army Medical Corps.

Fame did not protect him from discrimination. In the 1950s he was refused when he tried to buy a home in Garden Grove, California. He went on to practice medicine in Southern California and to coach younger divers, including Olympic champions Bob Webster, Pat McCormick and Greg Louganis.
Lee died on December 2, 2016, at age 96. His papers are held at the University of Southern California.
keyFacts: 1920: Born August 1 in Fresno, California.
1947: M.D., University of Southern California.
1948: Olympic gold (10 m platform) and bronze (3 m springboard) in London.
1952: Second platform gold, in Helsinki.
1953: Sullivan Award.
2016: Died December 2, age 96.

people.name: Young Oak Kim
body: In 1943 the commander of the 100th Infantry Battalion, a unit of Japanese Americans from Hawaii, offered a newly commissioned Korean American lieutenant a transfer, saying "Koreans and Japanese don't always get along." Korea was under Japanese colonial rule at the time. Young Oak Kim refused: "They're Americans, I'm American, and we're going to fight for America." He went on to become one of the battalion's most respected officers.

Kim was born in Los Angeles in 1919 to Korean immigrants Soon Kwon and Nora Koh Kim and grew up in the Bunker Hill neighborhood. He enlisted in January 1941 and was the only Asian American in his officer candidate class at Fort Benning. In Italy he earned a Silver Star and a Purple Heart. Near Anzio, in 1944, he led a daring daylight intelligence mission that earned him the Distinguished Service Cross. He was wounded again in France, at Biffontaine, and received the Croix de Guerre. In 2005 France upgraded that honor to the Legion of Honor.

He came home to Los Angeles and started a business, but he reenlisted in 1950. In the Korean War he became the first Asian American to command a regular U.S. combat battalion in war, the 1st Battalion, 31st Infantry Regiment. His battalion adopted a Seoul orphanage. He retired as a colonel in 1972.

In civilian life Kim helped build institutions for several Asian American communities. He was a founding member of the Korean American Museum and the Korean American Coalition, founding vice chairman of the Japanese American National Museum, and a co-founder of the Go For Broke Educational Foundation in 1989, which honors Japanese American veterans. He died in Los Angeles on December 29, 2005. UC Riverside's Young Oak Kim Center for Korean American Studies carries his name.
keyFacts: 1919: Born in Los Angeles to Korean immigrant parents.
1941: Enlisted in the U.S. Army.
1944: Distinguished Service Cross for an intelligence mission near Anzio, Italy.
Korean War: First Asian American to command a regular U.S. combat battalion in war.
1972: Retired as a colonel.
2005: Died December 29 in Los Angeles.

people.name: Herbert Y. C. Choy
body: On April 23, 1971, a Korean American lawyer from Hawai'i received his commission as a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. By the account of his Honolulu Advertiser obituary and the Congressional Record, Herbert Choy was the first Asian American to serve on the federal bench.

Choy was born on January 6, 1916, in Makaweli, a sugar plantation town on Kaua'i. His parents were part of the first waves of Korean immigrants to Hawai'i. On January 13, 1903, 102 Koreans had arrived in Honolulu to work on the islands' plantations. At 14, the Advertiser reported, he worked ten hours a day in a Honolulu pineapple plant. He earned a B.A. from the University of Hawai'i in 1938 and a J.D. from Harvard Law School in 1941. In November 1941 he became the first lawyer of Korean ancestry admitted to the bar in the United States. After Pearl Harbor he served in the Hawaii Territorial Guard and then the U.S. Army.

After the war he practiced law in Honolulu with Hiram Fong and Katsuro Miho. He served as Attorney General of the Territory of Hawai'i in 1957 and 1958. In 1971, President Richard Nixon nominated him to the Ninth Circuit. He took senior status in 1984 and kept serving until his death on March 10, 2004.
keyFacts: 1916: Born January 6 in Makaweli, Kaua'i, Hawai'i.
1941: J.D., Harvard Law School; admitted to the bar in November.
1957–1958: Attorney General of the Territory of Hawai'i.
1971: Commissioned to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.
1984: Took senior status.
2004: Died March 10 in Honolulu.

people.name: Grace K. Lee
body: "No matter what, we are going to survive," Grace Lee said in a Korean American Story Legacy Project video, interviewed by her daughter, Marie Myong-Ok Lee. She was reflecting on her decision to stay in the United States after considering a return to Korea, despite the difficulties she faced.

A 2007 release from the governor's office says Lee founded the Korean Service Center in Minneapolis, where she developed cross-cultural programs for elderly immigrants. The same release lists her as a teaching specialist, field instructor and consultant with the University of Minnesota's School of Social Work, and as a member of the Minneapolis Public Housing Authority.

The center still serves Korean seniors and the wider Korean community in Minnesota. It held a 35th anniversary celebration on September 25, 2026, which points to a start around 1991. Its own pages list 24-hour customized living, language support, help with government benefits, citizenship and residency, senior health programs, housing services and caregiver support.

Lee's work also reached state policy. She had been a member of the Minnesota Board on Aging since 2003, and in June 2007 Governor Tim Pawlenty reappointed her to a four-year term ending January 3, 2011. She died on May 4, 2025.

people.name: Marilyn Strickland
body: On January 3, 2021, Marilyn Strickland took office in the U.S. House of Representatives for Washington's 10th District. She was the first member of Congress of both Korean and African American heritage, and one of the first three Korean American women elected to Congress.

Strickland was born in Seoul, South Korea, on September 25, 1962. Her father was an African American soldier who fought in World War II and Korea, where he met her Korean mother. When she was a child the family moved to Tacoma, Washington, where he was stationed at what was then Fort Lewis.

She graduated from Mount Tahoma High School in Tacoma in 1980, earned a B.A. from the University of Washington in 1984 and an MBA from Clark Atlanta University in 1992. She worked as a marketing executive, including in management at Starbucks, before entering politics. After two years on the Tacoma City Council she became mayor in 2010, the first Asian-born person and the first Black woman to hold the office. From 2018 to 2019 she was president and CEO of the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, a post she left to run for Congress.

She won the seat in 2020 and became the first African American to represent Washington state, and the Pacific Northwest, in federal office. She has served on the Armed Services and Transportation and Infrastructure committees and has worked on pay and housing allowances for junior enlisted servicemembers. As of October 2026 she is in Congress and seeking a fourth term in the November 3, 2026, election.
keyFacts: 1962: Born September 25 in Seoul, South Korea.
1984: B.A., University of Washington. 1992: MBA, Clark Atlanta University.
2008–2009: Tacoma City Council.
2010: Became mayor of Tacoma.
2018–2019: President and CEO, Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce.
2020: Elected to the U.S. House; took office January 3, 2021.
2026: Seeking a fourth term in the November election.

people.name: Nam June Paik
body: On New Year's Day 1984, television viewers in New York and Paris watched the same live, chaotic, joyful show at once, beamed by satellite. It was called Good Morning, Mr. Orwell, a playful answer to George Orwell's novel 1984, which had warned that television would be a tool of control. The artist behind it, Nam June Paik, wanted to show that the same technology could connect people across the world.

Paik was born on July 20, 1932, in Seoul, while Korea was under Japanese colonial rule. He trained as a classical pianist. In 1950, during the Korean War, his family fled the country and eventually settled in Japan. He earned a degree in aesthetics from the University of Tokyo in 1956 and moved to West Germany in 1957 to study music. There he met the composer John Cage and joined Fluxus, an international group of artists who cared more about process and experience than finished objects. In 1963 his first exhibition, in Wuppertal, West Germany, filled a gallery with altered television sets.

In 1964 Paik moved to New York City. He was among the first artists to use the Sony Portapak portable video recorder, and he began a long collaboration with the cellist Charlotte Moorman; their works included TV Cello (1971), a cello made of stacked television sets. With engineer Shuya Abe he built the Paik/Abe video synthesizer in 1969, and his 1973 tape Global Groove became hugely influential. In TV Buddha (first version 1974), a statue sits watching its own live image on a screen. His 1995 neon-and-television map of the United States, Electronic Superhighway: Continental U.S., Alaska, Hawaii, was his gift to the Smithsonian American Art Museum, which holds it today.
A stroke in 1996 left him partly paralyzed, but he kept working. He died in Miami on January 29, 2006. He is often called the father of video art.
keyFacts: 1932: Born July 20 in Seoul, under Japanese rule.
1950: Family fled Korea during the Korean War.
1963: First exhibition, in Wuppertal, West Germany.
1964: Moved to New York City.
1984: Good Morning, Mr. Orwell satellite broadcast, January 1.
1996: A stroke left him partly paralyzed; he kept working.
2006: Died January 29 in Miami.

people.name: Margaret Cho
body: In 1994 ABC aired All-American Girl, a sitcom built on the stand-up comedy of a young Korean American woman from San Francisco. The Television Academy describes it as the first network comedy to feature an all-Asian-American cast. It lasted one season. Margaret Cho later spoke openly about how hard it had been, including network pressure over her appearance, and turned that experience into some of her most important work.

Cho was born on December 5, 1968, in San Francisco, to Korean immigrant parents who owned a bookstore near Haight-Ashbury. She began performing stand-up at 16, and in the early 1990s she won the American Comedy Award for Best Female Comedian, which led to the sitcom.

After the show ended, she wrote and performed a one-woman show, I'm the One That I Want, about the sitcom, body image, addiction and recovery. New York magazine named it a performance of the year. It became a concert film in 2000 and a book in 2001. Her 2005 essay collection, I Have Chosen to Stay and Fight, turned to politics and human rights.

Cho has been a long-time advocate for LGBTQ rights and marriage equality. She has received the GLAAD Golden Gate Award, honors from Lambda Legal and the ACLU of Southern California's First Amendment Award. In 2012 she received an Emmy nomination for a guest role on 30 Rock, and her comedy recordings have earned five Grammy nominations, from 2002 to 2017.
keyFacts: 1968: Born December 5 in San Francisco to Korean immigrant parents.
1994: Starred in ABC's All-American Girl.
2000–2001: I'm the One That I Want as a concert film, then a book.
2005: I Have Chosen to Stay and Fight.
2012: Emmy nomination, Outstanding Guest Actress in a Comedy Series (30 Rock).
2002–2017: Five Grammy nominations for comedy albums.

people.name: Susan Ahn Cuddy
body: After the attack on Pearl Harbor, a young Korean American woman in Los Angeles tried to join the Navy's women's reserve, the WAVES. Her first application was turned down because of her race. She kept applying, was accepted in 1942, and became the first Asian American woman to serve in the U.S. Navy. Susan Ahn went on to become the Navy's first female gunnery officer, training pilots to fire at targets in the air.

Ahn was born in Los Angeles in 1915, the oldest of five children. Her father was Ahn Chang-ho, known as Dosan, a leader of the Korean independence movement against Japanese colonial rule. Her parents immigrated to the United States in 1902. Her father was arrested by Japanese authorities in 1937 and died the next year.

She graduated from San Diego State College in 1940, enlisted in the WAVES in December 1942, completed officer training in 1943, and rose to lieutenant. She was assigned to the Office of Naval Intelligence, where she worked as a code-breaker and as its liaison with the Library of Congress. She left the Navy in 1946 and married Chief Petty Officer Francis Cuddy, a fellow intelligence specialist. She then worked at the National Security Agency, where during the Cold War she was an intelligence analyst and section chief supervising a large group of experts on Russian affairs. She left the intelligence community in 1959, when the couple moved to Los Angeles.

Back in California, she helped her siblings, including her brother Philip Ahn, run the family's Moongate Restaurant in Panorama City. In 2003 the California State Assembly named her Woman of the Year for its 28th District, and in 2006 she received the American Courage Award from the Asian American Justice Center. She died at home in Northridge, California, on June 24, 2015, at age 100.
keyFacts: 1915: Born in Los Angeles; daughter of independence leader Ahn Chang-ho.
1942: Joined the U.S. Navy in December, the first Asian American woman to do so.
1946: Left the Navy as a lieutenant.
Cold War: Intelligence analyst and section chief at the National Security Agency.
1959: Left the intelligence community and moved to Los Angeles.
2015: Died June 24 in Northridge, California, at age 100.

people.name: Sung Y. Kim
body: In October 2011 the United States appointed a new ambassador to South Korea who had been born in Seoul. Sung Kim had grown up in Los Angeles, and he returned as America's top diplomat there. The Korea Times called him the first U.S. ambassador to Korea with a Korean background.

Kim was born in Seoul in 1960. His family emigrated to the United States in the 1970s, and he grew up in Los Angeles. He earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Pennsylvania in 1982, a law degree from Loyola in 1985 and a master of laws from the London School of Economics in 1986. He first worked as a prosecutor in Los Angeles before joining the U.S. Foreign Service.

Much of his career centered on the Korean Peninsula and North Korea's nuclear program. He headed the State Department's Korea office, and in July 2008, The Korea Times reported, he became special envoy to the Six-Party Talks. He was ambassador to South Korea from 2011 to 2014, then served in Washington as Special Representative for North Korea Policy.

He went on to serve as ambassador to the Philippines (2016 to 2020) and to Indonesia (from October 2020). In 2021 he was also acting Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs for several months, and was named special representative for North Korea again. USC's Korean Studies Institute calls him the first Asian American to hold three U.S. ambassadorships. In 2024 he joined the Korean law firm Bae, Kim & Lee, and the institute lists him as president of Hyundai Motor Company since 2025.
keyFacts: 1960: Born in Seoul; grew up in Los Angeles.
2011–2014: U.S. ambassador to South Korea.
2016–2020: U.S. ambassador to the Philippines.
October 2020: Became U.S. ambassador to Indonesia.
2024: Joined Bae, Kim & Lee.
2025: Became president of Hyundai Motor Company.

people.name: Chloe Kim
body: In February 2018, a 17-year-old from Southern California won Olympic gold in snowboard halfpipe in Pyeongchang, South Korea, her parents' home country. Chloe Kim became the youngest woman to win an Olympic snowboarding gold.

Kim was born in 2000 in Long Beach, California, and her hometown is Torrance. Her parents, Jong Jin and Boran Kim, moved to the United States from South Korea. Her father took her snowboarding at age four, bought her a secondhand board and drove her to Mammoth Mountain on weekends.

She won her first X Games gold in superpipe in 2015, at age 14, the youngest winner in the event's history at that time, and went on to tie Shaun White for the most halfpipe wins in X Games history, with eight. In 2019 she announced a break from competition to attend Princeton University, then returned to the sport. At the 2022 Beijing Olympics she won halfpipe gold again, the first woman to win back-to-back Olympic halfpipe titles.

At the 2026 Milano Cortina Games, Kim competed with an injured shoulder after a crash in Switzerland about a month earlier. She led after her first run but fell on her last two. Gaon Choi of South Korea, a 17-year-old she had mentored, won gold, and Kim took silver.
keyFacts: 2000: Born in Long Beach, California; hometown Torrance.
2015: First X Games superpipe gold, at age 14.
2018: Olympic halfpipe gold in Pyeongchang at 17.
2022: Second Olympic halfpipe gold, in Beijing.
2026: Olympic silver in Livigno (Milano Cortina Games), February 12, behind Gaon Choi of South Korea.

people.name: Mia Mingus
body: Mia Mingus was born in 1980 in Busan, Korea, which she spells Pusan in her oral history. At six months old she was adopted to St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands, where she grew up until she was 17. She went to Agnes Scott College in Georgia and stayed in the Atlanta area for 13 years, organizing there. At 26 she became co-executive director of SPARK Reproductive Justice NOW.

She later moved to the Bay Area and joined the Bay Area Transformative Justice Collective, which works on community responses to child sexual abuse that do not rely on police or prisons. She describes herself as a "queer physically disabled Korean woman transracial and transnational adoptee." The White House named her a Champion of Change for Asian and Pacific Islander women. In her oral history she recalls using a wheelchair at a crowded national march that she calls "totally not accessible."

people.name: Catherine Enz
body: In April 2024 Catherine Enz wrote to the Minnesota Senate Judiciary and Public Safety Committee in support of S.F. 5097, a bill on the rights of parents with disabilities. This entry draws only on that public testimony, in which she introduces herself in her own words.

She writes that she was adopted from South Korea at seven months old by two parents who are both completely blind. She grew up in Edina, went to Hamline University and earned a graduate degree at the University of Minnesota. She describes herself as a healthcare industry professional and a disability justice advocate.

Asked throughout her life what it is like to have blind parents, she answers by asking what it is like to have sighted parents. Her parents, she writes, may have done things in a different way, but the public assumes that their way is worse "simply because they cannot imagine doing it without vision."
keyFacts: Adopted from South Korea at seven months; raised in Edina, Minnesota.
Hamline University; MPH, University of Minnesota.
April 2024: Wrote in support of S.F. 5097.

institutions.name: Korean Culture Camp of Minnesota
body: In 1977 Korean Culture Camp of Minnesota held its first session for Korean adoptees. VOA Learning English reports that it was started by parents of adopted Korean children, who wanted their children to understand the country and culture they had left behind and to feel good about their Korean heritage.

The camp grew out of one of the largest adoption stories in the country. Korean adoption in Minnesota began in 1955 through Children's Home Society. Children's Home Society started a formal Korean adoption program in 1967, and Lutheran Social Services followed in 1969. MNopedia reports that adoptees make up almost half of Minnesota's Korean American population, in a passage that discusses 2017 data; it gives no exact year or count for that share.

Korean Culture Camp is one of several such camps in the state, alongside Kamp Kimchee, Camp Choson and Camp Moon Hwa. It was incorporated as a Minnesota nonprofit in July 1987. VOA reported that enrollment peaked at about 700 in the 1990s and had more recently been 250 to 300 children a summer, run largely by parent volunteers and teen helpers. Today the camp says it serves adoptees and their siblings, children of former adoptees, first-generation Korean Americans and others. It has set its 2027 camp for July 19 to 23, with a 50th-year celebration on July 24.
keyFacts: 1955: First Korean adoptions in Minnesota.
1977: First Korean Culture Camp of Minnesota.
1967 and 1969: Formal Korean adoption programs begin at Children's Home Society (1967) and Lutheran Social Services (1969).
July 1987: Incorporated as a Minnesota nonprofit.
1990s: Enrollment peaked at about 700, by VOA's report.
July 2027: 50th-year celebration planned.

institutions.name: Koreatown Youth and Community Center
body: On February 14, 1975, the Korean Youth Center opened in Los Angeles with one staff member, as an outreach project of the Asian American Drug Abuse Program. It became an independent nonprofit in 1983, added "Community" to its name in 1992 and took its current name in 2004.

Its neighborhood had changed fast. Between 1970 and 1980, KYCC reports, the Korean American population of the area grew about 700 percent, from 8,500 to more than 60,000. Following the unrest that began on April 29, 1992, known as Sa-I-Gu, KYCC reports that 2,280 Korean American businesses were looted and burned. KYCC then added a neighborhood economic development program to help small business owners.

KYCC says its mission is to serve the changing needs of Korean Americans in greater Los Angeles and the multiethnic Koreatown community, with a focus on recently immigrated, low-income youth and families. It offers mental health counseling, family support, drug and alcohol recovery services, supportive housing, financial help, youth and college-prep programs, environmental programs and resources on anti-Asian hate. It reports 13 locations across Koreatown.
keyFacts: 1975: Opened as the Korean Youth Center.
1983: Became an independent nonprofit.
1992: Added a neighborhood economic development program after Sa-I-Gu.
2004: Renamed Koreatown Youth and Community Center.
Reports 13 locations across Koreatown.

institutions.name: Koreatown, Los Angeles
body: In 1982 Koreatown signs went up near the 10 freeway and Normandie Avenue in Los Angeles. The neighborhood had been officially recognized two years earlier, in 1980.

Korean immigrants began arriving in California in the early 1900s. Ahn Chang-ho and his wife came to San Francisco in 1902, and after a 1913 freeze hurt the citrus industry the family moved to Los Angeles, where Korean communities grew around institutions such as the Korean Presbyterian Church. Racial covenants and economic barriers kept Koreans in a few districts until the covenants were struck down in 1948. The Korean National Association, a key organization of the independence movement, moved its main headquarters from San Francisco to Los Angeles in 1936.

The modern Koreatown took shape after the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965. In the late 1960s, falling property values in the mid-Wilshire area drew Koreans to buy homes and businesses there. In 1968 Hi Duk Lee opened the Olympic Market, and he later built a plaza of Korean-owned businesses at Olympic Boulevard and Normandie Avenue. By the end of the 1980s, KYCC reports, the neighborhood had hundreds of churches, dozens of newspapers and a 24-hour radio station.

The 1992 unrest, known as Sa-I-Gu, destroyed much of the neighborhood. UCLA's Asian American Studies Center puts the toll at 2,280 stores and about $400 million in losses, nearly half of the city's total. On May 2, 1992, a crowd marched for peace in Koreatown, calling for healing between Korean and African American residents. L.A. TACO reports that more than half of the neighborhood's residents today are Latino, and about two-thirds were born outside the United States.
keyFacts: 1936: Korean National Association moved its main headquarters to Los Angeles.
1968: Hi Duk Lee opened the Olympic Market.
1980: Koreatown officially recognized; signs installed in 1982.
1992: Sa-I-Gu; 2,280 stores and about $400 million in losses, by UCLA's account; peace march May 2.

institutions.name: Korean American Special Education Center
body: Rosa Chang, whose Korean name is Chang Kyung Hae, co-founded the Korean American Special Education Center in 2000 with behavioral clinicians and social workers. The goal, by the Korean American Story's profile of her, was to serve Korean Americans with developmental disabilities in Los Angeles who could not get care in their language. The profile names her as executive director. Chang says she studied in the United States because Korea offered little acceptance of or education on developmental disabilities when she was young, and that community awareness has grown since then, but slowly.

KASEC works in Los Angeles and Orange County, with centers in Los Angeles and Cypress. It offers developmental screenings, behavioral consultations, after-school and inclusive programs, family support and Korean-language seminars for parents. In a 2018 grant application to the California Department of Developmental Services, it described itself as the first Korean American special-needs resource center in the country. Its site showed new workshops and events in September and October 2026.
keyFacts: Founded 2000.
Centers in Los Angeles and Cypress, California.
Korean-language seminars for parents.

institutions.name: CIDA Community Center
body: Dr. Young Seh Bae has a doctorate in special education from Teachers College, Columbia University, and a child on the autism spectrum. In 2013 she started a support group for Korean parents of children with developmental disabilities. The Community Inclusion & Development Alliance became a state-recognized nonprofit in 2016, and the next year began receiving federal funding as a Parent Resource Center.

CIDA offers support groups organized by language and age, one-on-one translation, advocates who go to school meetings with families, job training for young adults, daily-living-skills workshops and an art cooperative. QNS reported in December 2023 that it serves about 1,500 families, mostly in Queens, and that it is the only parent center serving Korean Americans in the country. Its site lists an art exhibition and an annual gala for late 2026.
keyFacts: 2013: Began as a parent support group.
2016: Became a state-recognized nonprofit.
About 1,500 families, by QNS's 2023 report.
Based on Bell Boulevard, Bayside, Queens.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Korean Minnesotans include immigrant families and their U.S.-born children, and Korean adoptees, most of whom were raised by non-Korean families. Most of the research below is about immigrant families and may not apply to adoptees at all. We found no Minnesota study of Korean families and disability. Two Minnesota-relevant figures are not disability studies as such. A University of Minnesota study (Keyes et al., 2008) assessed 514 international adoptees, most born in South Korea per NPR's report, alongside domestic adoptees and nonadopted teens in Minnesota. It found most adopted teens psychologically healthy, with roughly double the odds of contact with a mental health professional and of a disruptive behavior disorder. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports a Korean disability rate of 5.5 percent, and 5.0 percent under age 65. The studies are few, small, set mainly in Los Angeles or New York, and in some cases available only in summary.
questions: How do you describe yourself: Korean immigrant, U.S.-born Korean American, Korean adoptee, or in some other way?
How do you and those close to you understand what's going on? What words do you use for it?
What have you been told, or what do you think, about why this happened? You don't have to answer that if you would rather not.
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it to you, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a disability label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you would want it to avoid?
Would you like information in Korean, an interpreter, or English? If you would like an interpreter, what would make one comfortable for you?
Does a church, pastor, parent group or community organization help you? Would you like us to work with them, or keep them out of it?
Who should be part of decisions about your services, and who should not?
What are your long-term hopes, such as where you or your young person will live and what work you might do?
Is there anything about how others in your community might see this that you want us to be careful about?
If you were adopted, are there records, citizenship papers or family history questions that make this process harder?

context.heading: What one survey asked about autism
body: A University of California, Los Angeles survey presented at a 2018 autism research meeting asked 159 Korean adults, recruited at Korean community organizations in Los Angeles, about autism (Lee and Kasari). Answers about cause fell into four kinds: biological, parenting, postnatal and unsure. People who immigrated at older ages knew less about autism and were more likely to name parenting as a cause. People who immigrated younger, had a family member with autism, or were women knew more.

In that sample, answers varied with age at immigration and personal experience. It is a conference poster from one city and says nothing about any one family. If someone raises parenting as a cause, offer clear information without blame.

sources.label: Lee and Kasari, International Society for Autism Research (2018), poster abstract

context.heading: Families and planning for adulthood
body: A 2007 interview study with 10 Korean American parents of adolescents with disabilities (Kim, Lee and Morningstar) named five themes: how parents perceived disability, advocacy, expectations for future living, connections with Korean communities, and partnerships with professionals. The available summary names the themes but does not report what parents said about them, so we cannot tell you what those views were. Its authors urge educators to involve parents in long-range planning. Ask about hopes for adult life early.

A 2015 review (Choi and Ostendorf) notes that U.S. data on Korean American students with disabilities is not recorded separately and is counted within "Asian American." Be careful with any figure offered as being about Korean American students.

sources.label: Kim, Lee and Morningstar, Research and Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities (2007), abstract
Choi and Ostendorf, Journal of the American Academy of Special Education Professionals (2015), abstract and introduction

context.heading: Churches, help-seeking and mental health
body: This study is about mental health, not disability, so apply it with care. Baek and colleagues (2024) surveyed 243 Korean American adults, 110 church leaders and 133 members, at seven churches in greater Los Angeles from November 2017 to February 2018, using a convenience sample. Reviewing earlier work, they say Korean Americans underuse mental health services, often as a last resort, and that churches can be pillars of support. They cite another study's estimate that about 59 percent of Korean Americans identify as Christian.

In their sample, 53.4 percent of members and 43.6 percent of leaders said they confided in family or friends when distressed. The authors suggest that services work with churches and that pastors receive mental health training. Many Korean Minnesotans are not Christian, and an adoptee may have no tie to a Korean church. Involve a church or pastor only if the person wants that.

sources.label: Baek and colleagues, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2024)

context.heading: Adoption records and citizenship
body: MPR News reported in November 2025 that South Korea's government had admitted widespread corruption in hundreds of thousands of adoptions, including falsified paperwork and destroyed records. MPR calls Minnesota home to the largest population of Korean adoptees in the U.S. Do not treat an adoptee's records as complete or accurate, and offer another route when a process depends on them.

Some intercountry adoptees reach adulthood without U.S. citizenship, which can affect eligibility for public benefits. Adoptees United reports that its Citizenship Clinic had received 496 requests for help and served 447 people as of October 2026. Those are the clinic's own figures, for adoptees from 46 countries and not only from Korea.

sources.label: MPR News, "Mistaken: Minnesota's Korean adoptees grapple with confessed systemic corruption" (November 2025)
Adoptees United

context.heading: Words, and who has organized
body: 장애인 (jang-ae-in) is used for a disabled person in the title of the Korean translation of a University of Kansas guide to respectful language. Check any other Korean term, including 장애우, with a qualified interpreter or a Korean disability organization; we did not find a source on how acceptable those terms are. Follow each person's own words. Mia Mingus, profiled on this page, uses "physically disabled."

Parents and professionals have built much of the organizing we could document. KASEC and CIDA, profiled on this page, are examples. Catherine Enz, also profiled here, describes growing up as a Korean adoptee with two blind parents and argues that disability does not make someone a bad parent. Do not treat any one person or organization as speaking for everyone.

context.heading: What we could not find
body: We did not find a source we could read on fate, karma, ancestral or spiritual explanations of disability in Korean American families, so do not assume them. We also found none on gender roles in caregiving, on who makes decisions, or on traditional Korean medicine in disability care. Ask who should be part of decisions.

We did not find a Minnesota Korean disability organization, though the search was limited. The Korean Service Center is not a disability-specific agency, but it runs 24-hour customized living, caregiver support and in-home supports.

communityRoutes.purpose: A Christian ministry in Roseville for Korean adoptees and families, with wellness and mental health programs. For people who want a faith-based setting.

organizations.intro: Minnesota's Korean community has two large strands: first-generation immigrants and their families, and Korean adoptees, whom MPR News calls the largest such population in the U.S. A 2020 Korean Quarterly review of Sooh-Rhee Ryu's book Koreans in Minnesota names the Korean American Association of Minnesota, the Korean Institute of Minnesota and the Korean Service Center among the community's organizing efforts. We could not find a Minnesota-based Korean-language newspaper, radio program or channel, so ask the Korean Service Center or the association which channels people use. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.
